name: Battle of Yamen
info: A Yuan fleet under Zhang Hongfan defeated the chained Song fleet in the bay at Yamen in southern China on 19 March 1279, ending the Song dynasty; the child emperor Zhao Bing died in the sea.

facts.date: 19 March 1279, after a blockade and an assault prepared on 18 March
facts.place: The bay at Yamen (also called Yashan), now in the town of Yamen, Xinhui County, Jiangmen, Guangdong, southern China
facts.sides: The Southern Song under Zhang Shijie and the prime minister Lu Xiufu, with about 1,000 ships chained together and many non-combatants; the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty under Zhang Hongfan, reinforced by Li Heng
facts.outcome: The Song fleet was overwhelmed and the boy emperor Zhao Bing died in the sea, which effectively ended the Song dynasty and left the Yuan under Kublai Khan with all of China

t: Zhang Shijie had about 1,000 ships chained together in the bay, with the emperor's boat in the centre, to stop individual ships from fleeing, but the chained ships could neither support the middle nor retreat.
The Yuan cut the Song off from fresh water and wood on land, and the Song soldiers were forced to eat dry foods and drink sea water, which caused nausea and vomiting.
Zhao Bing was the last Song emperor, and his death effectively ended the Song dynasty and left the Yuan under Kublai Khan with all of the country.
dyk: Zhang Shijie had the palaces, houses and forts on land burned so that his soldiers could not flee the battle, and Yuan sailors lulled the Song with festive music before the attack.
ev: The Southern Song court flees Lin'an, leaving Emperor Gong to be captured, and Zhao Shi is declared emperor
Fuzhou falls to the Yuan, and the court flees towards Quanzhou, where Pu Shougeng refuses it boats
Zhao Shi dies and is succeeded by Zhao Bing, aged seven, whom Zhang Shijie brings to Yamen; Wen Tianxiang is captured
Zhang Hongfan, reinforced by Li Heng, attacks the Song navy at Yamen, and Zhang Shijie has about 1,000 ships chained together
The Yuan blockade the bay and the Song run out of supplies, and Zhang Hongfan prepares an assault on 18 March
The Yuan overwhelm the Song fleet, and Lu Xiufu jumps into the sea with the boy emperor, and both drown
Dowager Yang takes her own life at sea, and Zhang Shijie is assumed to have drowned in a tropical storm

sections.background:
In 1276 the Southern Song court, hurrying to flee the capital Lin'an as Yuan forces approached, left Emperor Gong behind to be captured. Hopes of resistance centred on his two young brothers, and the older, Zhao Shi, was declared emperor. When Fuzhou fell to the Yuan in 1277, the exiled court fled to Quanzhou, where the Grand General of Song, Zhang Shijie, hoped to borrow boats. The Muslim merchant Pu Shougeng refused, so Zhang confiscated his properties and left on stolen boats with the court. In fury, Pu slaughtered imperial clan members and many officials in Quanzhou and surrendered to the Yuan, which strengthened Yuan naval power.

The Song no longer had the strength to risk a head-on conflict with the Yuan. Zhang Shijie decided to build a vast fleet from what remained, so that the court and the soldiers could move from place to place until the situation improved. The court sailed from Quanzhou to Guangdong, but Zhao Shi's boat capsized in a storm on the way to Leizhou. He survived but fell ill, and the court later took refuge at Mui Wo on Lantau Island, where he died. His younger brother Zhao Bing, who was seven, succeeded him, and Zhang Shijie brought the new emperor to Yamen and prepared its defence against the Yuan. In 1278 Wen Tianxiang, who had fought the Yuan in Guangdong and Jiangxi, was captured by Wang Weiyi in Haifeng County, which removed all the Song land forces nearby.
sections.forces:
The Song side was a fleet carrying a court. Zhang Shijie commanded it, with the seven-year-old Zhao Bing as emperor and Lu Xiufu as prime minister, and it held many non-combatants as well as soldiers. Some within the Song forces suggested that the navy first take the mouth of the bay, to secure a line of retreat to the west. Zhang turned this down so that his soldiers could not flee the battle, and he also ordered all the palaces, houses and forts on land burned for the same reason. He had about 1,000 ships chained together in a long string within the bay, with Zhao Bing's boat in the centre of the fleet, again to stop individual ships from fleeing. All the Song ships had been painted with fire-resistant mud.

The Yuan attack was led by Zhang Hongfan, reinforced by Li Heng, who had earlier captured Guangzhou. The Yuan navy blockaded the bay while the Yuan army cut off the Song's fresh water and wood on land. Zhang Hongfan decided against using cannons, since they could break the chains of the formation too effectively and let the Song ships retreat. Before the assault he divided his naval forces into four parts: one each for the Song's east, north and south sides, while he led the remainder to about a li from the Song forces.
sections.course:
The Yuan first steered fire ships into the Song formation, but the Song ships were prepared for such an attack. The blockade then did its work. The Song side, with its many non-combatants, soon ran out of supplies, and its soldiers were forced to eat dry foods and drink sea water, which caused nausea and vomiting. Zhang Hongfan kidnapped Zhang Shijie's nephew and asked him three times to surrender, without result. In the afternoon of 18 March he prepared a massive assault.

On 19 March the north flank engaged the Song forces first and was repulsed. The Yuan then began playing festive music, which led the Song to think the Yuan were holding a banquet and to lower their guard. At noon Zhang Hongfan attacked from the front, with additional soldiers hidden under large pieces of cloth. When his boats neared the Song fleet, the Yuan sounded the horn of battle and the soldiers under the fabric were revealed. The Song had prepared for a small skirmish. Waves of arrows hit the Song ships and the fleet at once lost seven ships and many troops.

The ill and weakened Song soldiers were no match for the Yuan in close combat, and in the chaos command was impossible. The chained ships could neither support the middle nor retreat. Seeing the battle lost, Zhang Shijie picked his finest soldiers, cut about a dozen ships out of the formation and tried to break out to save the emperor. The Yuan reached the centre and Zhao Bing, killing everyone in their way. Lu Xiufu, seeing no hope of breaking free, took the boy emperor with him into the sea, where both drowned. Many officials and concubines followed.
sections.aftermath:
After the Song troops were killed, the slaughter of the Song court began. The History of Song records that seven days after the battle thousands of corpses floated to the surface of the sea. The body of the boy emperor was reportedly found near what is now Shekou in Shenzhen, though his actual grave has not been found.

Zhang Shijie escaped the battle. He hoped to have Dowager Yang appoint the next Song emperor and to continue resisting the Yuan from there, but when she heard of the emperor's death she also took her own life at sea, and Zhang buried her on the shore. He and his remaining soldiers were assumed to have drowned, since a tropical storm rose soon afterwards. There have been suggestions that his death was Mongol propaganda, since no remains or trace of his fleet were ever found.

As Zhao Bing was the last Song emperor, his death effectively ended the Song dynasty, and the House of Zhao lost power over China altogether. The Yuan dynasty under Kublai Khan held all the country. Kublai Khan and his successors ruled China for 97 years, until the rise of the Ming dynasty under the Hongwu Emperor.
sections.sources:
The History of Song records that seven days after the battle thousands of corpses floated to the surface of the sea.

Some points are uncertain. The Song fleet is put at about 1,000 ships. Zhao Bing's actual grave has not been found, and his body was only reportedly found near Shekou. The fate of Zhang Shijie is also in doubt. He and his soldiers were assumed to have drowned in the storm, but because no remains or trace of his fleet were ever found, it has been suggested that his death was simply Mongol propaganda.
sections.legacy:
The battle is considered the last stand of the Song dynasty against the Yuan, and it ended the Song. The conquest of the south completed Yuan rule over all of China, which lasted until the Ming under the Hongwu Emperor, when the Chinese regained control of the lost territory from the Mongols.

The defeat also left a mark on those who had been on the Song side. Pu Shougeng went over to the Yuan, but towards the end of the Yuan dynasty the Yuan Mongols turned against his family and the Muslims and killed his descendants in the Ispah rebellion. Mosques and other buildings of foreign architecture were almost all destroyed.

At the site a rock was carved in memory of Zhang Hongfan. Many temples were built in the surrounding area in memory of those who lost their lives in the last years of the Song, among them Wen Tianxiang, Lu Xiufu and Zhang Shijie. In the 1980s another memorial was built near Shekou to commemorate Zhao Bing. The Teochew people remember the boy emperor through the preparation of a leafy greens soup, patriotic soup. A museum complex, the Song-Yuan Yamen Sea Warfare Culture Tourist Zone, lies just east of the battle site.

summary: At Yamen on 19 March 1279 a Yuan fleet under Zhang Hongfan overwhelmed the Song fleet, chained together in the bay, after a blockade had cut off its water. The boy emperor Zhao Bing died in the sea, which effectively ended the Song dynasty.
notes: The article gives no strength for the Yuan or a total for the Song beyond 'about 1,000 ships'; the sections say so only in forces and sources, briefly.
The aftermath names 'Emperor Huaizong' as the emperor whose death Dowager Yang heard of; the article never calls Zhao Bing that, so I wrote 'the emperor's death'.
The sources section is thin: the article names only the History of Song; I wrote no claim about eyewitnesses or later accounts.
The sentence 'the Yuan imperial soldiers killed most of the descendants of Pu Shougeng and horrifically mutilated their corpses' was shortened and the mutilation left out.
Fire ships: the article does not say how the attack ended, only that the Song ships were prepared; I wrote that it failed, which is implied.
The article names Li Heng as having captured Guangzhou earlier; kept. Wang Weiyi and Haifeng kept as given.
The article's 'Pu slaughtered imperial clan members' and the conquest by the Mongols are given as the article has them.
